metadata.title: Examining the relationship between online chatting and PISA reading literacy trends (2000-2018)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA reading literacy and questionnaire-based indicators aggregated to the country level for 39 countries across PISA cycles from 2000 to 2018. For preparatory multilevel trend estimation and for constructing country-level aggregates (e.g., reading literacy averages and percentages), the authors weight student responses using the PISA sampling weight W_FSTUWT, which indicates how many students each sampled respondent represents. To avoid overrepresentation of large countries and to prevent miscalculation of statistical significance, the authors compute standardized country weights (WEIGHT) based on the average population size represented by each country across years, and use these standardized weights in the main correlation/path analyses. Replicate weights are not reported, and the analysis is conducted at the country-unit level (39 records), so the weighting is used to reflect population representativeness rather than to compute BRR/jackknife variance estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not describe a specific missing-data handling procedure for the country-level trend-change dataset used in the main correlations/path analysis. While it states there were no missing data at the country level for the trend-change variables (and that yearly averages/percentages could always be obtained), it does not document how missingness at the student level within PISA was handled before aggregation (e.g., whether nonresponse was treated via PISA’s standard procedures or excluded cases). This is a reporting gap because the study relies on stable country-level estimates derived from student-level PISA data.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses PISA reading literacy and related questionnaire indicators aggregated at the country level for 39 countries. The included countries are those that participated in the first PISA survey (2000/2002), with two countries excluded from PISA 2000 and one excluded from PISA 2002; Liechtenstein is excluded after not meeting participation requirements beyond 2012, the Netherlands is excluded for not meeting PISA sample requirements, and Romania is excluded due to a strongly deviating age range. The study includes all available PISA reading literacy measurements from 2000 to 2018 (up to seven measurements per country), but online chatting and reading fiction are only available in specific reading-focused years (chatting: 2009 and 2018; fiction: 2000/2002, 2009, 2018). For reading strategies, only changes during 2009–2018 are used because strategy questions were collected only in 2009 and 2018. The main dataset for correlations/path analysis contains 39 country records (one per country) with computed trend-change variables; the paper reports no missing data at the country level for these trend-change values.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2000–2018 Reading literacy (15-year-olds; country-level trend changes after 2009)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Path analysis (lavaan) on 39 countries weighted by standardized country weights: Online chatting → Reading literacy (standardized coefficient −0.378, p=0.009); Reading fiction → Reading literacy (0.219, p=0.005); Reading strategies → Reading literacy (0.386, p=0.007). Model accounts for 64.1% of the variance in reading literacy trend changes; overall fit: χ² p=0.998; TLI≈1.000; RMSEA/SRMR reported as favorable (exact values not provided in excerpt).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2000–2018 Reading literacy the study leveraged online chatting trend change, reading fiction trend change, and reading strategies awareness change (plus robustness controls such as internet availability and reading time) to explain reading literacy trend change at the country level, finding that increases in online chatting growth after 2009 coincided with decelerations in reading literacy trends and that this association was partially mediated by changes in reading fiction and reading strategies. This indicates that education policy should prioritize supporting sustained reading practices (fiction) and explicit instruction in effective reading strategies to buffer reading literacy declines in increasingly digital environments, while noting that the evidence is correlational and based on country-level aggregates rather than individual causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes country-level trend changes in PISA reading literacy for 15-year-olds across 2000–2018, focusing on shifts after 2009. The authors first estimate per-country reading literacy trend changes using multilevel modeling with cross-sectional repeated measures, then compute correlations and a path model (lavaan) among four focal constructs: online chatting trend change, reading fiction trend change, reading strategies awareness change (available only for 2009–2018), and reading literacy trend change. Across 39 countries (weighted by standardized country weights derived from W_FSTUWT), the strongest correlation is between online chatting and reading literacy trend changes (r = −0.698, p < 0.001). In the path model, online chatting has a negative direct effect on reading literacy (β = −0.378, p = 0.009), while reading fiction and reading strategies have positive effects (β = 0.219, p = 0.005; β = 0.386, p = 0.007). The model explains 64.1% of variance and shows favorable fit (χ² p = 0.998), but the design is correlational and uses country aggregates, so causal claims about individual students cannot be inferred.
